metrics.name: Price of GPT-4-level AI (cheapest model scoring at least 86 on MMLU)

source.title: Epoch AI, LLM inference prices have fallen rapidly but unequally across tasks (Cottier et al., 2025), lowest_price_models_data.csv

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: The cheapest model that matches the original GPT-4 (March 2023) on MMLU (score of 86 or more), at its release date, from Epoch AI's CSV (https://epoch.ai/data/charts/llm-inference-price-trends/lowest_price_models_data.csv, updated November 2025, downloaded 2026-10-28). Price is a 3:1 blend of input and output token prices, the first-party API price where there is one. Epoch's data ends with models released in February 2025. Epoch found prices for a fixed capability falling 9 to 900 times a year depending on the benchmark (about 40 times a year at GPT-4 level on PhD-level science questions). Its later study, "The plunging price of thought" (September 2026, https://epoch.ai/publications/the-plunging-price-of-thought), uses cost per answered question instead and finds about 13 times a year overall. MMLU is near saturation and may be partly memorised, so cheap models can match GPT-4 on it while being weaker on harder tasks.

metrics.name: Time horizon of frontier AI agents on software tasks (METR, 50% success)

source.title: METR, Time horizons of frontier AI models (Time Horizon 1.1 results, benchmark_results_1_1.yaml)

metrics.license: Copyright METR, all rights reserved (no open license stated); figures reused as cited facts
metrics.note: The length of software, research-engineering and cybersecurity tasks, measured by how long they take skilled humans, that a model completes with 50 percent probability. Only models METR marks as state of the art at release are kept (18 of 26), dated by release. Values are METR's Time Horizon 1.1 estimates (228 tasks, after METR's correction of 3 March 2026), from https://metr.org/assets/benchmark_results_1_1.yaml, downloaded 2026-10-28; TH1.1 revised several older models (GPT-4 from 6.0 to 4.0 minutes, GPT-5 from 131 to 203). METR's own doubling time from 2023 on is about 129 days (CI 104 to 158), and about 188 days over the whole series. METR says estimates above 16 hours are unreliable with the current task suite, so the last two points (12 and 17 hours) have very wide intervals, and its page says it is no longer actively updated: no model released after April 2026 had been measured by October 2026. A 50 percent horizon is not the same as doing the job reliably; METR's 80 percent horizons are about 4 to 8 times shorter.

metrics.name: Training compute of notable AI models

source.title: Epoch AI, Notable AI Models dataset

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: Exact values from Epoch AI's notable_ai_models.csv, downloaded 2026-10-27. Most frontier values after 2022 are Epoch estimates, not lab disclosures, and the confidence labels range from confident to speculative. Epoch finds frontier training compute growing about 4 to 5 times per year since 2010 (https://epoch.ai/blog/training-compute-of-frontier-ai-models-grows-by-4-5x-per-year).

metrics.name: Price of lithium-ion battery packs (BloombergNEF survey average)

source.title: BloombergNEF, Lithium-ion battery pack prices fall to $108 per kilowatt-hour, despite rising metal prices (December 2025), and New record lows for battery prices

metrics.license: Copyright BloombergNEF; headline figures from its public press releases, reused as cited facts
metrics.note: Volume-weighted average price of a finished pack (cells plus modules, battery management, wiring and housing; for stationary storage, the rack) across electric cars, buses, commercial vehicles, two- and three-wheelers and stationary storage, all restated by BNEF in real 2025 dollars. 2013 to 2025 are the labelled bars of BNEF's 2025 survey chart (lithium_11.png in the press release); 2010 is from the line chart in "New record lows for battery prices" (https://about.bnef.com/insights/clean-transport/new-record-lows-for-battery-prices/), whose caption gives $1,474 (written "$!,474"). BNEF restates the whole history every year, so older releases quote smaller numbers for the same years (for example $1,100 for 2010 in the 2020 survey). Segment prices are lower than the average: in 2025, stationary storage packs averaged $70, car packs $99 and all packs in China $84. The cell share of the 2025 average was $74.

metrics.name: World cereal yield

source.title: Our World in Data, Cereal yield (FAO, Production: Crops and livestock products, 2025)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: World production of all cereals (wheat, rice, maize, barley, sorghum, millet and others) divided by harvested area, from FAOSTAT via OWID (CSV downloaded 2026-10-28). Rice is counted as paddy. The rise from 1.35 tonnes in 1961 to over 4 is the Green Revolution and its successors: semi-dwarf wheat and rice, hybrid maize, fertilizer and irrigation. Growth has been roughly linear (about 0.045 tonnes a year), so the exponential fit slowly overstates future gains.

metrics.name: Price of gene synthesis per base

source.title: Rob Carlson, DNA cost and productivity data, aka 'Carlson curves' (synthesis.cc, 26 October 2022)

metrics.license: Carlson's figures are CC BY-ND 4.0; the tabulated prices are reused as cited facts. 2026 point from Twist Bioscience's public price page.
metrics.note: Price to the customer of double-stranded synthetic genes, in nominal US dollars per base, as tabulated by Carlson (1999 to 2017). 2026 is Twist Bioscience's list price for gene fragments (https://www.twistbioscience.com/products/genes: "from $0.07/bp", rising to $0.09 for 3 to 5 kb and $0.09 to $0.23 for cloned genes); GenScript lists cloned genes from $0.15 a base. Carlson's 2016 and 2017 values ($0.03 and $0.02) are lower than any list price found today and may reflect bulk contracts, so the curve has in practice been flat at about $0.07 to $0.15 for list-price genes since about 2014. Short column-synthesized oligos fell much more slowly, from $1 a base (1992) to $0.05 (2017) in the same table; array-synthesized oligo pools are far cheaper, which Carlson (2025) puts at $0.00001 to $0.001 a base, but need assembly and error correction to make genes.

metrics.name: Price of computer memory (RAM) per gigabyte

source.title: Our World in Data, Historical cost of computer memory and storage (John C. McCallum, 2023, adjusted with the US CPI)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0 (OWID processing); underlying compilation by John C. McCallum
metrics.note: Cheapest retail or catalogue price McCallum found each year for main memory (magnetic core before the mid-1970s, then DRAM chips and modules), converted by OWID to constant 2020 US$ with the US consumer price index, and here from dollars per terabyte to dollars per gigabyte (4 significant figures). OWID CSV downloaded 2026-10-28; the series ends in 2023. McCallum's original site (jcmit.net) no longer serves his tables. DRAM prices are cyclical, so single years can sit well off the trend.

metrics.name: Record fusion triple product in magnetic confinement

source.title: Wurzel and Hsu, Continuing progress toward fusion energy breakeven and gain as measured against the Lawson criterion, Physics of Plasmas 32, 112106 (2025), arXiv:2505.03834

metrics.license: Paper under the arXiv non-exclusive license; the underlying dataset (github.com/swurzel/lawson-criterion-paper) is MIT-licensed
metrics.note: The Lawson triple product n_i0 T_i0 tau_E* (peak ion density times peak ion temperature times energy confinement time, corrected for transient heating), the record for magnetic confinement devices (tokamaks, pinches, stellarators) by year, from Tables 1 to 3 of Wurzel and Hsu (2025) and their 2022 paper (arXiv:2105.10954). By their Table 3 (2022), D-T ignition needs at least 2.9e21 keV·s/m³ at 14 keV, and Q_fuel = 1 needs 4.6e20. The magnetic record has stood since TFTR in 1995: JT-60U reached 5.6e20 in 1998 and JET 2.2e20 in its 2021 D-T campaign, and the machines designed to pass ignition (SPARC, projected 6.2e21; ITER, projected 7.4e21) are still being built. The best stellarator is Wendelstein 7-X at 6.2e19 (2017); its 2025 long-pulse record had no published value at the time of checking. Inertial confinement uses a different triple product (n ⟨T⟩ tau_stag) and a different ignition condition, so it is not mixed in: NIF holds that record at 1.7e22 (shot N170827, 2017), and its shot N210808 (2021) reached hot-spot ignition at 1.6e22. After ignition the triple product stops being a useful measure for ICF; NIF's later shots are measured by gain (Q_sci 1.51 in December 2022, 4.13 in April 2025).

metrics.name: GPU price-performance (FP32 FLOP/s per dollar, record-setting GPUs)

source.title: Epoch AI, Machine Learning Hardware dataset

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: Computed from Epoch AI's ml_hardware.csv (downloaded 2026-10-27) as FP32 peak FLOP/s divided by release price in nominal USD, keeping only GPUs that set a new record; the dataset has few priced consumer GPUs after 2022. ML accelerators are better measured in tensor FP16/FP8, where price-performance is higher (for example H100 SXM at about 2.9e10 dense FP16 FLOP/s per dollar and GB200 at about 6.8e10). Epoch's 2022 study of 470 GPUs found FP32 FLOP/s per dollar doubling about every 2.5 years, and every 2.07 years for GPUs used in ML (https://epoch.ai/blog/trends-in-gpu-price-performance).

metrics.name: Price of hard disk storage per gigabyte

source.title: Our World in Data, Historical cost of computer memory and storage (John C. McCallum, 2023, adjusted with the US CPI)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0 (OWID processing); underlying compilation by John C. McCallum
metrics.note: Cheapest price McCallum found each year for hard disk drives (IBM's RAMAC in 1956 onward), converted by OWID to constant 2020 US$ with the US consumer price index, and here from dollars per terabyte to dollars per gigabyte (4 significant figures). OWID CSV downloaded 2026-10-28; the series ends in 2023. The decline has slowed since about 2010, from halving every 1 to 2 years to every 4 or so.

metrics.name: Cost to launch a kilogram to low Earth orbit (cheapest vehicle available)

source.title: CSIS Aerospace Security Project (2022), via Our World in Data, Cost of space launches to low Earth orbit

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0 (OWID processing); underlying data CSIS
metrics.note: The record line of the cheapest vehicle available: of the 60 vehicles in the CSIS table (first flights 1962 to 2019), only those whose cost per kilogram beat every earlier vehicle are kept, dated by first successful launch. Cost is the price of a dedicated launch divided by the vehicle's LEO payload capacity, in constant 2021 US$. Earlier versions of this file plotted every vehicle; small rockets cost 5 to 30 times more per kilogram at any date, so that cloud had no usable trend (r² 0.14). The record line stalled from 1967 to 2010 and then fell fast with SpaceX. These are list prices for fully expendable payload capacity; SpaceX's internal cost with booster reuse is lower, but not published. The CSIS table ends in 2019 (OWID checked 2026-10-28) and has no Starship point. Original CSIS page: https://aerospace.csis.org/data/space-launch-to-low-earth-orbit-how-much-does-it-cost/

metrics.name: Record life expectancy at birth (best country each year)

source.title: Our World in Data, Life expectancy at birth (Riley 2005; Zijdeman et al. 2015; Human Mortality Database 2025; UN World Population Prospects 2024)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: The highest period life expectancy at birth (both sexes) among countries and territories with at least 1 million people that year, computed from the OWID life expectancy and population CSVs downloaded 2026-10-28; every fifth year to 1985, then every year to 2023. The population floor leaves out microstates such as Monaco and San Marino, whose UN estimates sit 1 to 2 years above any large country. This is the record line Oeppen and Vaupel (Science 296, 1029, 2002) drew, which rose about 3 months a year from 1840; they used women's life expectancy, which runs a few years higher. The leader passed from Sweden and Norway to Australia, Japan (1980s to 2010s) and Hong Kong. COVID-19 interrupted the rise in 2020 to 2022. The trend fitted here is exponential like every other series, but the classic description is a straight line.

metrics.name: Price of lithium-ion battery cells (cells only, not packs)

source.title: Our World in Data, Price of lithium-ion battery cells (Rupert Way 2026, based on Ziegler and Trancik 2021, BloombergNEF and Avicenne Energy)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0 (as published by Our World in Data)
metrics.note: The price of CELLS only, not packs (see battery-pack-price for finished packs; BNEF's 2025 pack average was $108/kWh, of which $74 was cells). Representative cell price across major chemistries, constant 2024 US$ per kWh. 1991 to 2015 follow Ziegler and Trancik (2021, Energy Environ. Sci. 14, 1635); later years blend BloombergNEF and Avicenne survey data. 1991 to 2024 are rounded to 1 decimal from the OWID CSV (downloaded 2026-10-27, unchanged on 2026-10-28). 2025 is the cell share in BNEF's 2025 survey chart (real 2025 US$; that chart also puts 2024 cells at $78, so the two dollar bases agree closely): https://about.bnef.com/insights/clean-transport/lithium-ion-battery-pack-prices-fall-to-108-per-kilowatt-hour-despite-rising-metal-prices-bloombergnef/

metrics.name: Labor price of light

source.title: Nordhaus (1996), "Do Real-Output and Real-Wage Measures Capture Reality? The History of Lighting Suggests Not", in Bresnahan and Gordon (eds.), The Economics of New Goods (NBER, University of Chicago Press), Table 1.6; series as published by Our World in Data

metrics.license: Our World in Data's processing is CC BY 4.0. The underlying figures are from Nordhaus's NBER chapter (copyright University of Chicago Press); they are reused here as cited facts.
metrics.note: Labor hours an average worker needed to earn the price of 1,000 lumen-hours (about one 60-watt incandescent bulb burning for an hour) with the best common technology of each date. US wage data from 1800 on; earlier points are rough reconstructions. The lamp labels are inferred from Nordhaus's text and may not match every row exactly.

metrics.name: Cost to sequence a human genome

source.title: NHGRI DNA Sequencing Costs Data (Sequencing_Cost_Data_Table_May2022.xls)

metrics.license: public domain
metrics.note: NHGRI Genome Sequencing Program production costs, all 78 data points as published (Sept 2001 to May 2022; page last updated May 16, 2023). Years are fractional: each point is dated to the end of its month (for example 2001.75 is 2001-09-30). Values are in nominal US dollars, rounded to the cent. A 'genome' is 3,000 Mb at the coverage of the era's dominant platform (about 6x Sanger before 2008, about 30x short reads after), and costs include labor, reagents, instrument depreciation, informatics and overhead, but not assembly or analysis. The cliff from late 2007 to 2009 is the switch from capillary Sanger to second-generation sequencers. The May 2022 point repeats the February 2022 value in the source. NHGRI has not published newer data (checked 2026-10-28). Vendor list prices for reagents are lower than these all-in production costs: about $200 a genome for Illumina's NovaSeq X (2022) and about $80 claimed by Ultima for its Solaris chemistry (2025). The trend is fitted from mid-2015 on, when cost halving slowed to about every five years.

metrics.name: Cost per megabase of DNA sequence

source.title: NHGRI DNA Sequencing Costs Data (Sequencing_Cost_Data_Table_May2022.xls)

metrics.license: public domain
metrics.note: NHGRI Genome Sequencing Program production costs, all 78 data points as published (Sept 2001 to May 2022; page last updated May 16, 2023). Years are fractional: each point is dated to the end of its month (for example 2001.75 is 2001-09-30). Values are nominal US dollars per million bases of raw sequence, rounded to six significant figures. Sanger-era data counts Phred Q20 bases; second-generation data uses each platform's own quality threshold. Moore's law (halving every two years) would have taken $5,292 to about $4 by mid-2022; the actual figure is about $0.006, roughly 700 times lower.

metrics.name: Levelized cost of electricity from new solar PV plants, world

source.title: Our World in Data, Levelized cost of energy by technology (IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2025, and earlier editions)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0 (OWID); IRENA data may be reused with attribution
metrics.note: Levelized cost of electricity: lifetime cost of building, financing and running a plant divided by its lifetime output, without subsidies, as estimated by IRENA in constant 2025 US$ (4 significant figures, OWID CSV downloaded 2026-10-28). Global capacity-weighted average for utility-scale solar PV plants commissioned each year. The fall slowed after 2020: LCOE was flat at about 0.043 from 2023 to 2025.

metrics.name: Cumulative installed solar capacity, world

source.title: Our World in Data, Installed solar energy capacity (IRENA Renewable Energy Statistics 2026)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: Total solar capacity, on- and off-grid, as reported by IRENA. It includes concentrated solar power, which is under 1 percent of the total (roughly 7 GW), so it can stand in for cumulative PV. Values rounded to 2 decimals from the OWID CSV downloaded 2026-10-27. Series starts in 2000; IRENA's figures are AC or DC depending on the country.

metrics.name: Solar photovoltaic module price

source.title: Our World in Data, Solar photovoltaic module price (IRENA Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2024 and in 2025; Nemet 2009; Farmer and Lafond 2016)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: Module price only, excluding installation and balance of system. Nemet (2009) for 1975 to 2003, Farmer and Lafond (2016) for 2004 to 2009, IRENA's global module price index (pvXchange benchmark for modules sold in Europe) for 2010 to 2019, and IRENA's "mainstream" crystalline silicon module series from 2020 (OWID joins the two without rescaling; they differ by under 20 percent in 2020 to 2023). Deflated to 2025 US$ by OWID with the World Bank US GDP deflator. Values rounded to 4 decimals from the OWID CSV downloaded 2026-10-28 (OWID revised the series on 2026-10-23, which lowered 2024 from 0.27 to 0.13). Paired with solar-pv-cumulative-capacity for a Wright's law fit (price drop per doubling of cumulative capacity).

metrics.name: Transistors in the largest microprocessor

source.title: Our World in Data, Moore's law: the number of transistors per microprocessor (from Rupp, Microprocessor Trend Data, 2022)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0 (OWID); later points CC BY-SA 4.0 (Wikipedia)
metrics.note: 1971 to 2021 are the OWID series (downloaded 2026-10-27), rounded to whole transistors, keeping only years where the record changed; OWID's source (Rupp) ends in 2021. 2022, 2023 and 2026 are the largest counts in the microprocessor table of Wikipedia's "Transistor count" article (read 2026-10-28; CC BY-SA 4.0). Since about 2019 the record holders are multi-chip packages (AMD's Epyc Rome in 2019 already was), so the series measures transistors per processor package, not per die. GPUs, which are not in this series, are larger still (Nvidia's two-die B200, 2024, about 208 billion).

metrics.name: Best two-qubit quantum gate error rate

source.title: Sevilla and Riedel, Forecasting timelines of quantum computing (arXiv:2009.05045, dataset CC BY 4.0), plus the papers named on each point

metrics.license: Dataset CC BY 4.0; later points are published results reused as cited facts
metrics.note: The lowest two-qubit entangling gate error reported each time the record fell, on any platform; so far every record has been set with trapped ions. Papers measure it differently (Bell-state fidelity, randomized benchmarking, IonQ's leakage-aware benchmarking), so points are only roughly comparable, and a best pair in a lab is better than a whole machine's average (Quantinuum's commercial H1-1 averaged 8.6e-4 in 2024; superconducting fluxonium reached 7.8e-4 in 2023, Ding et al., PRX 13, 031035; neutral atoms 5e-3 in 2023, Evered et al., Nature 622, 268). The 2003 point is from Sevilla and Riedel's spreadsheet (https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/1pwb4gf0FxlxgfVhtXTaqEGS9b7FwsstsJ0v7Zb1naQ0/). Error correction needs physical errors well below the surface-code threshold of about 1e-2, across many more qubits than any of these records used.

metrics.name: Wheat yield in England and the United Kingdom

source.title: Our World in Data, Wheat yields (FAO 2025; Broadberry et al. 2015; Brassley 2000; Bayliss-Smith and Wanmali 1984)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0
metrics.note: Harvested wheat per hectare in England (medieval and early modern points, Broadberry et al., British Economic Growth 1270-1870) and the United Kingdom (from 1887; FAO from 1961). Early points are averages over decades. From 1961 to 1999 only every fifth year is kept; every year from 2000. OWID CSV downloaded 2026-10-28. Yields roughly doubled between 1300 and 1800, nearly tripled by 1961, and then doubled again by the late 1990s with semi-dwarf varieties, fertilizer and fungicides; the national average has been flat at 7 to 9 tonnes since the late 1990s, with weather-driven dips (2001, 2012, 2020, 2024).

metrics.name: Levelized cost of electricity from new onshore wind farms, world

source.title: Our World in Data, Levelized cost of energy by technology (IRENA, Renewable Power Generation Costs in 2025, and earlier editions)

metrics.license: CC BY 4.0 (OWID); IRENA data may be reused with attribution
metrics.note: Levelized cost of electricity: lifetime cost of building, financing and running a plant divided by its lifetime output, without subsidies, as estimated by IRENA in constant 2025 US$ (4 significant figures, OWID CSV downloaded 2026-10-28). Global capacity-weighted average for onshore wind farms commissioned each year; IRENA's series starts in 1984. The fall has flattened since about 2021.
